title: Understand and Participate in Change Management Processes
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 7: Security Operations: Understand and Participate in Change Management Processes.

items: Request — formal submission of the proposed change with justification
Review — assess the impact, risk, and resource requirements of the change
Approve/Reject — change advisory board or authorized individual makes the decision
Test — validate the change in a non-production environment
Implement — deploy the approved and tested change during a maintenance window
Document — record all details of the change: what, when, who, why, outcome
Post-implementation review — verify the change achieved its objectives without unintended consequences
Change management processes help prevent outages by ensuring changes are reviewed, approved, and tested before deployment
Ensures that changes are documented — critical for disaster recovery (e.g., administrators can review logs to see what changed recently)
Rollback plan — every change should have a documented plan to reverse it if problems occur

blocks.text: Change management is a foundational operations security process. Without proper change management, unauthorized or poorly tested changes can introduce vulnerabilities, cause outages, or create configuration drift. A change log should track all approved changes. It can be manually created or generated from an internal system as personnel record activity related to a change. Change logs are useful for tracking approved changes and are also helpful as part of a disaster recovery program — administrators can review the change logs to identify recent changes that may have contributed to a failure. Emergency changes (e.g., critical security patches for actively exploited vulnerabilities) may follow an expedited process, but they should still be documented after the fact and reviewed by the CAB in the next regular meeting.

items: CAB — committee responsible for reviewing and approving/rejecting proposed changes
Composition: representatives from IT, security, business units, and management
Evaluates: technical feasibility, business impact, risk, resource requirements, scheduling
Emergency CAB (ECAB) — smaller group with authority to approve emergency changes quickly
Central repository of information about IT assets and their configurations
Tracks configuration items (CIs) — hardware, software, documentation, and their relationships
Essential for: change impact analysis, incident investigation, disaster recovery planning
Every installed application and service must be part of the CMDB so vulnerabilities can be tracked
Integration with change management — all changes should update the CMDB
